entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Eastern Orthodox Church is the second-largest Christian church in the world with approximately 260 million members, tracing its origins to the early Christian communities established by Christ's apostles and developing as the established church of the Byzantine Empire. The Great Schism of 1054 CE, when mutual excommunications between Pope Leo IX and Patriarch Michael Cerularius divided Christianity into Western (Catholic) and Eastern (Orthodox) branches, remains unhealed after nearly a millennium.

The Orthodox Church developed as the spiritual center of Byzantine civilization, commissioning Hagia Sophia (537 CE) — the greatest cathedral of the ancient world — and spreading Christianity to Russia, Serbia, Bulgaria, Romania, and Georgia through missionary work. Cyril and Methodius, 9th-century Byzantine missionaries, created the Cyrillic alphabet for Slavic languages, transforming the cultural map of Eastern Europe and enabling Orthodox Christianity's spread.

Orthodox Christianity's autocephalous structure — national churches (Greek, Russian, Serbian, Romanian, etc.) each governed by their own patriarch — means there is no single Orthodox pope, creating both decentralization and political complexity. The Russian Orthodox Church, with 100+ million adherents, is the largest Orthodox body. The Russian Church's support for Vladimir Putin's regime and blessing of the Ukraine war (2022) created the deepest Orthodox internal split since the Great Schism, with the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople recognizing the independent Ukrainian Orthodox Church in 2019.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Eastern Orthodox Church shaped Byzantine and Slavic civilizations, created the Cyrillic alphabet, and remains central to the cultural identity of Russia, Greece, and Eastern Europe — with its current split over Ukraine reflecting orthodoxy's unresolved political tensions.
